desc:
Given an unsorted integer array nums (it may contain zero, negative numbers and repeats) and a positive integer k, return the k smallest positive integers that do not appear in nums, in increasing order.

For example, nums = [3, -1, 4, 1] and k = 3 give [2, 5, 6], because 1, 3 and 4 are present while 2, 5 and 6 are the first three absent positive integers.
hints: Positive integers are checked in order 1, 2, 3, ... Which data structure makes 'is v in nums?' a constant-time question?
Put the values in a hash set, then count upward from 1 and collect each number that is not in the set.
How far can the counter go? At most n numbers are blocked by the array, so the k-th missing positive is at most n + k, which means the loop is short enough to run directly.
editorial: Insert all values into a set. Then iterate c = 1, 2, 3, ...; whenever c is not in the set, append it to the answer, and stop once k numbers are collected.

The loop runs at most n + k times: among the integers 1..n+k at most n can be present in the array, so at least k are missing. The total cost is O(n + k) time and O(n) space. The classic follow-up places each value v in the range 1..n at index v - 1 by swapping (cyclic sort), which removes the set; the first indices where nums[i] != i + 1 then reveal the missing numbers below n, and the rest are found by counting past n while skipping the displaced extra values.
